A 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of
progressively worsening right scrotal pain. He says the pain started 3 days ago when he woke
up. At first, the pain was a minor annoyance, but it has gradually increased in intensity to the
point that it is now somewhat uncomfortable to walk. He has also noted a gradual swelling of his
right scrotum but denies penile discharge, urinary frequency, dysuria, hematuria, or fevers. He
denies any trauma to the area. He competed in a basketball game the previous evening but did
not feel as though he strained himself during the game. He denies experiencing anything like
this in the past. He has taken acetaminophen for the scrotal pain without any relief.

A 34-year-old man presents to urgent care after twisting his left ankle while stepping off a curb earlier today. He describes an inversion mechanism and reports hearing a crack at the time of injury. He is unable to bear weight on the left foot. He denies any previous ankle injuries. On examination, there is significant swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus. Point tenderness is present over the distal fibula with palpable bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus. The medial malleolus is nontender. Anterior drawer test of the ankle is difficult to assess due to pain and guarding. Neurovascular status of the foot is intact with brisk capillary refill and intact sensation. Ankle radiographs demonstrate a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) with no talar shift.

A 68-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of mild heart failure comes to the office because of a
1-week history of dyspnea on exertion. He is relatively sedentary but is usually able to climb a
flight of stairs without stopping. Now he must stop every few steps to rest because of dyspnea
but not chest discomfort. He also complains of lower extremity edema, 2-pillow orthopnea,
cough with occasional production of white phlegm, wheezing, and a 3-kg weight gain. He denies
chest pain or discomfort, palpitations, syncope or near syncope. He has had no fever or upper
respiratory symptoms. He states he has been compliant with his medications and denies any
changes to his diet. He was seen by another physician two times in the past few months for
similar symptoms; both times he had an ECG and chest x-ray and was told he had "mild heart
failure." He was treated with an increased dose of furosemide without any other workup.

A 20-year-old female college student presents with bilateral itchy, watery eyes for the past 3 days. She reports that the symptoms began shortly after spring pollen counts increased. She has a known history of seasonal allergies but has not yet started any medications this year. She denies eye pain, photophobia, purulent discharge, or changes in vision. On examination, bilateral conjunctival injection is noted with mild chemosis. There is clear watery discharge. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual acuity is intact bilaterally. There is no preauricular lymphadenopathy.

A 10-year-old girl is brought in by her parents who report she frequently feels nauseated and dizzy during car rides, particularly on winding roads. Symptoms have been occurring for the past year and typically resolve within 15 to 20 minutes after stopping the vehicle. She does not vomit. Sitting in the front seat and looking out the window helps somewhat. She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, or similar symptoms outside of car rides. On examination, she is well-appearing and in no distress. Vital signs are age-appropriate. Neurological exam, including cranial nerves and cerebellar testing, is normal. Otoscopic exam is unremarkable.

The burning typically occurs 30 to 60 minutes after large meals, particularly those that are spicy or high in fat. The discomfort is relieved within minutes by over-the-counter antacids. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. He has no cardiac history. On examination, vital signs are normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. There is no epigastric tenderness. Cardiac exam is unremarkable.

A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain that is constant and dull. She reports low-grade fever and mild nausea but no vomiting. She had a colonoscopy 2 years ago that showed extensive diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon. Her diet is low in fiber. She reports one episode of constipation followed by loose stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.8°F, heart rate 86, blood pressure 128/76. On examination, there is moderate tenderness in the left lower quadrant with voluntary guarding but no rebound tenderness or rigidity. Bowel sounds are present and hypoactive. There is no palpable mass. Laboratory work shows a white blood cell count of 13,200 with a left shift. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrates sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolic fat stranding and no abscess or perforation.

A 32-year-old male singer presents with a hoarse voice that has persisted for 3 days following an intense concert performance. He reports mild sore throat and throat dryness but denies dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, fever, or hemoptysis. He is a non-smoker and does not consume alcohol regularly. He has no history of GERD or thyroid disease. On examination, he is afebrile. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without exudates or lesions. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. His voice is notably hoarse and breathy. Respiratory effort is normal with no stridor or wheezing on auscultation.

A 20-year-old female college student who recently started a running program presents with bilateral dull, aching pain along the front of both shins. The pain began about 1 week ago and occurs primarily during and shortly after running, then resolves with rest. She runs on paved surfaces in her current athletic shoes that are over a year old. She denies pain at rest, nighttime pain, swelling, or history of stress fractures. On examination, there is mild tenderness on palpation along the medial border of the bilateral tibias spanning approximately 5 cm. There is no point tenderness, edema, or erythema. Ankle range of motion and strength are normal.

A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.

A 29-year-old male software developer presents with eye fatigue, dryness, and a mild headache that worsens throughout the workday. He spends 10 to 12 hours daily in front of computer screens and often forgets to take breaks. He reports that symptoms improve on weekends when he reduces screen time. He denies blurred vision, floaters, flashes of light, or eye pain. He does not wear corrective lenses. On examination, visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally. Extraocular movements are intact. Pupils are equal and reactive. Conjunctivae are mildly injected. The anterior segment and fundoscopic exams are normal bilaterally.

Cervical lymph nodes are not enlarged. She is well-appearing and in no distress.

A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother who noticed multiple itchy red bumps on his arms and legs after he spent the afternoon playing outside in the backyard. The bumps appeared over the past 24 hours. He has been scratching but the mother reports no significant swelling beyond the immediate area of each bump. He denies fever, joint pain, or any recent travel. On examination, there are approximately 8 to 10 small erythematous papules, each 3 to 5 mm in diameter, scattered on the bilateral forearms and lower legs. Several have small central puncta. There is no surrounding cellulitis, lymphangitis, or regional lymphadenopathy.

episode of confusion. The day prior to her visit she attended a wedding at which she had "2 or
3" glasses of wine and afterwards felt extremely tired whereby she left early. When she got
home, she went straight to bed without even undressing. She awoke about 3 h later and didn't
remember going to bed or that she had just been at a wedding. Both arms were painful when
she awoke, and she noticed blood in her mouth. Her husband says she had been "tossing
around in bed." She returned to bed and awoke in the morning several hours past her usual
time. She and her husband thought these events were very unusual, and although she felt back
to normal except for some slight soreness in her arms, she decided to go the emergency
department.

A 68-year-old woman who has followed a strict vegan diet for the past 12 years presents with a 4-month history of progressive tingling and numbness in both feet, fatigue, and difficulty with balance. She reports her tongue has been sore intermittently. She has noticed increased forgetfulness and mild cognitive slowing. She takes no supplements. On examination, vital signs are normal. She appears pale with a smooth, beefy red tongue (glossitis). Neurological examination reveals diminished vibration and proprioception in both feet and ankles, absent ankle reflexes, and a positive Romberg sign. Gait is wide-based and mildly ataxic. Upper extremity neurological exam is normal. CBC reveals hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Peripheral blood smear shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum B12 level is critically low at 85 pg/mL (normal 200-900). Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels are both elevated.

He has a temperature of 38.3°C (101°F), a blood pressure of 144/92 mm Hg, a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, a heart rate of 90 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 92 percent while breathing room air. Physical examination reveals only crackles and egophony in the right lower lung field. The white-cell count is 14,000 per cubic millimeter, and the results of routine chemical tests are normal. A chest radiograph shows an infiltrate in the right lower lobe.

She recalls stepping on a nail while walking barefoot in her yard four days ago. She cleaned the wound at the time but did not seek medical attention. She reports low-grade fever and mild chills. On examination, vital signs are temperature 100.6°F, heart rate 84, blood pressure 142/88. The right foot shows a puncture wound on the plantar surface with surrounding erythema extending 6 cm, warmth, edema, and tenderness. There is no crepitus or fluctuance. Peripheral pulses are diminished bilaterally. Her last tetanus booster was over 10 years ago.

She had been experiencing nipple soreness and cracking on the right side and notes the baby has had difficulty latching on that side. She denies palpable masses or nipple discharge other than breast milk. Vital signs show temperature 101.2°F, heart rate 94, blood pressure 118/72. On examination, there is a wedge-shaped area of erythema, warmth, and induration in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. The area is exquisitely tender to palpation. There is no fluctuance or palpable abscess. The ipsilateral nipple shows a small fissure. Axillary lymph nodes are mildly enlarged on the right.

A 22-year-old sexually active man presents with a 4-day history of gradually worsening left scrotal pain and swelling. The pain is dull and aching and radiates to the left inguinal region. He reports mild dysuria and a small amount of urethral discharge noticed over the past week. He has had a new sexual partner in the past month and inconsistently uses barrier protection. He denies fever, nausea, vomiting, or testicular trauma. Vital signs are normal. On examination, the left hemiscrotum is swollen and erythematous. There is tenderness and induration localized to the left epididymis posterior to the testis. Prehn sign is positive with relief of pain on elevation of the left testis. The cremasteric reflex is present bilaterally. There is no testicular torsion on clinical assessment. Urinalysis shows 15 to 20 WBC per high-power field. A nucleic acid amplification test for chlamydia and gonorrhea is sent.

A 12-year-old boy is brought by his parents for a persistent cough that has lasted 3 weeks and is progressively worsening. The illness began with 1 week of runny nose and mild cough that was initially thought to be a cold. The cough then intensified into severe paroxysms of rapid, consecutive coughs followed by a whooping inspiratory sound. He has had several episodes of post-tussive vomiting. He occasionally turns red in the face during coughing fits. Between episodes he appears relatively well. His vaccination records show he received DTaP at 2, 4, and 6 months but missed his preschool and adolescent boosters. Vital signs are normal between episodes. Lungs are clear to auscultation. A nasopharyngeal swab PCR for Bordetella pertussis returns positive. CBC shows a white blood cell count of 18,000 with 70% lymphocytes.

A 62-yr-old man comes to his primary care clinic with the chief complaint of chest pain. He has
no pain currently. He first noticed the pain 2 mo ago but attributed it to indigestion. He describes
the pain as a pressure sensation in the middle of his chest that does not radiate anywhere else.
It seems to come only with exertion and not at rest. He noticed it more last week when he had to
shovel snow; he has had no pain since then. He says the pain usually lasts 10 to 15 min and
goes away if he takes a break. When present, the pain is not worsened by movement or
breathing. The last time he got the pain, he took an aspirin, which he thinks helped. The pain is
not associated with shortness of breath, nausea, or diaphoresis. He denies any recent fever,
cough, or infectious symptoms.

A 38-year-old obese woman presents with a 2-day history of worsening right upper quadrant pain that began after eating fried chicken. The pain is constant, radiates to her right scapula, and is associated with nausea and two episodes of nonbilious vomiting. She has had intermittent postprandial bloating and epigastric discomfort over the past year that she attributed to indigestion. She denies jaundice, dark urine, or pale stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, heart rate 92, blood pressure 130/84. On examination, she is moderately uncomfortable. There is tenderness in the right upper quadrant with a positive Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest during palpation of the RUQ). There is no rebound tenderness, rigidity, or palpable mass. Right upper quadrant ultrasound reveals a distended gallbladder with gallstones, wall thickening to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign. The common bile duct measures 4 mm.

A 34-year-old man presents to urgent care after twisting his left ankle while stepping off a curb earlier today. He describes an inversion mechanism and reports hearing a crack at the time of injury. He is unable to bear weight on the left foot. He denies any previous ankle injuries. On examination, there is significant swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus. Point tenderness is present over the distal fibula with palpable bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus. The medial malleolus is nontender. Anterior drawer test of the ankle is difficult to assess due to pain and guarding. Neurovascular status of the foot is intact with brisk capillary refill and intact sensation. Ankle radiographs demonstrate a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) with no talar shift.

A 56-year-old man presents to urgent care with acute onset of excruciating pain in his right great toe that woke him from sleep at 3 AM. The pain developed rapidly over several hours and is now the worst pain he has ever experienced, rated 10 out of 10. He reports the toe is so sensitive that even the weight of a bedsheet is unbearable. He had a steak dinner with several beers the evening before onset. His past medical history includes hypertension managed with hydrochlorothiazide and hyperlipidemia. He is overweight with a BMI of 30. On examination, the right first metatarsophalangeal joint is intensely erythematous, swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender to even light palpation. Active and passive range of motion is severely limited by pain. Vital signs show temperature 99.4°F, heart rate 88. Serum uric acid is 9.8 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers show ESR 42 and CRP 6.2.

A 28-year-old woman who is 3 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding presents with a 2-day history of increasing pain, redness, and swelling in her right breast. She reports associated fever and chills and feeling generally unwell. She had been experiencing nipple soreness and cracking on the right side and notes the baby has had difficulty latching on that side. She denies palpable masses or nipple discharge other than breast milk. Vital signs show temperature 101.2°F, heart rate 94, blood pressure 118/72. On examination, there is a wedge-shaped area of erythema, warmth, and induration in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. The area is exquisitely tender to palpation. There is no fluctuance or palpable abscess. The ipsilateral nipple shows a small fissure. Axillary lymph nodes are mildly enlarged on the right.

A 22-year-old sexually active man presents with a 4-day history of gradually worsening left scrotal pain and swelling. The pain is dull and aching and radiates to the left inguinal region. He reports mild dysuria and a small amount of urethral discharge noticed over the past week. He has had a new sexual partner in the past month and inconsistently uses barrier protection. He denies fever, nausea, vomiting, or testicular trauma. Vital signs are normal. On examination, the left hemiscrotum is swollen and erythematous. There is tenderness and induration localized to the left epididymis posterior to the testis. Prehn sign is positive with relief of pain on elevation of the left testis. The cremasteric reflex is present bilaterally. There is no testicular torsion on clinical assessment. Urinalysis shows 15 to 20 WBC per high-power field. A nucleic acid amplification test for chlamydia and gonorrhea is sent.

The illness began with 1 week of runny nose and mild cough that was initially thought to be a cold. The cough then intensified into severe paroxysms of rapid, consecutive coughs followed by a whooping inspiratory sound. He has had several episodes of post-tussive vomiting. He occasionally turns red in the face during coughing fits. Between episodes he appears relatively well. His vaccination records show he received DTaP at 2, 4, and 6 months but missed his preschool and adolescent boosters. Vital signs are normal between episodes. Lungs are clear to auscultation. A nasopharyngeal swab PCR for Bordetella pertussis returns positive. CBC shows a white blood cell count of 18,000 with 70% lymphocytes.

lightheadedness, or syncope. He denies any cough, fever, chills, or night sweats.

failure." He was treated with an increased dose of furosemide without any other workup.

A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain that is constant and dull. She reports low-grade fever and mild nausea but no vomiting. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrates sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolic fat stranding and no abscess or perforation.

A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.

Differential (%)

1-week history of dyspnea on exertion. He is relatively sedentary but is usually able to climb a

respiratory symptoms. He states he has been compliant with his medications and denies any
changes to his diet. He was seen by another physician two times in the past few months for
similar symptoms; both times he had an ECG and chest x-ray and was told he had "mild heart
failure." He was treated with an increased dose of furosemide without any other workup.

A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.

Differential (%)

Bands 4

Monos 4

A 68-year-old woman who has followed a strict vegan diet for the past 12 years presents with a 4-month history of progressive tingling and numbness in both feet, fatigue, and difficulty with balance. She appears pale with a smooth, beefy red tongue (glossitis). Neurological examination reveals diminished vibration and proprioception in both feet and ankles, absent ankle reflexes, and a positive Romberg sign. Gait is wide-based and mildly ataxic. Upper extremity neurological exam is normal. CBC reveals hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Peripheral blood smear shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum B12 level is critically low at 85 pg/mL (normal 200-900). Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels are both elevated.

A 38-year-old obese woman presents with a 2-day history of worsening right upper quadrant pain that began after eating fried chicken. The pain is constant, radiates to her right scapula, and is associated with nausea and two episodes of nonbilious vomiting. She has had intermittent postprandial bloating and epigastric discomfort over the past year that she attributed to indigestion. She denies jaundice, dark urine, or pale stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, heart rate 92, blood pressure 130/84. On examination, she is moderately uncomfortable. There is tenderness in the right upper quadrant with a positive Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest during palpation of the RUQ). There is no rebound tenderness, rigidity, or palpable mass. Right upper quadrant ultrasound reveals a distended gallbladder with gallstones, wall thickening to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign. The common bile duct measures 4 mm.

Serum B12 level is critically low at 85 pg/mL (normal 200-900). Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels are both elevated.

He has noted increased swelling in his legs. He denies any shortness of breath at rest,
orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. He denies any episodes of palpitations,
lightheadedness, or syncope. He denies any cough, fever, chills, or night sweats.

She denies pain at rest, nighttime pain, swelling, or history of stress fractures. On examination, there is mild tenderness on palpation along the medial border of the bilateral tibias spanning approximately 5 cm. There is no point tenderness, edema, or erythema. Ankle range of motion and strength are normal.

A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.

A 56-year-old man presents to urgent care with acute onset of excruciating pain in his right great toe that woke him from sleep at 3 AM. The pain developed rapidly over several hours and is now the worst pain he has ever experienced, rated 10 out of 10. He reports the toe is so sensitive that even the weight of a bedsheet is unbearable. He had a steak dinner with several beers the evening before onset. His past medical history includes hypertension managed with hydrochlorothiazide and hyperlipidemia. He is overweight with a BMI of 30. On examination, the right first metatarsophalangeal joint is intensely erythematous, swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender to even light palpation. Active and passive range of motion is severely limited by pain. Vital signs show temperature 99.4°F, heart rate 88. Serum uric acid is 9.8 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers show ESR 42 and CRP 6.2.

A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain that is constant and dull. She reports low-grade fever and mild nausea but no vomiting. She had a colonoscopy 2 years ago that showed extensive diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon. Her diet is low in fiber. She reports one episode of constipation followed by loose stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.8°F, heart rate 86, blood pressure 128/76. On examination, there is moderate tenderness in the left lower quadrant with voluntary guarding but no rebound tenderness or rigidity. Bowel sounds are present and hypoactive. There is no palpable mass. Laboratory work shows a white blood cell count of 13,200 with a left shift. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrates sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolic fat stranding and no abscess or perforation.

A 42-year-old woman comes to the office for evaluation of significant anemia. She was diagnosed the previous week at an urgent care center during an evaluation for a 2-week history of progressive fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. She had a negative workup for cardiac and pulmonary disease, including normal pulse oximetry, chest x-ray, ECG, and point-of-care cardiac ultrasound. However, at that visit her hemoglobin was discovered to be 7.0 gm/dL (70 gm/L). Today in the office, she is still dyspneic with exertion, is unable to climb a flight of stairs without stopping, but she denies any other current symptoms. She has noted no bloody or dark stools or excessive vaginal bleeding. Her menses are regular, lasting 4 days, and she describes them as "not heavy." She has been told in the past that she had a "low blood count" that her previous doctor attributed to her periods and her vegetarian diet. She was sometimes treated with iron supplements but has had no other treatment or workup.


She brings her CBC results from the urgent care center:

Hemoglobin (g/dL) 7.2
Hematocrit (%) 21.6
RBC (million/cm3) 3.5
WBC/ mm3 7500
Differential (%) 
Polys 75
Bands 4
Lymphs 15
Monos 4
Eosinophils 2
MCH (pg/cell) 30
MCV (fL) 89
MCHC % 39
RDW 13
